en: I, the Emperor, reflect that the Buddha-way is vast and profound, subtle and precise; its divine mystery responds and penetrates all.
It benefits all beings through compassion and awakens humanity through wisdom. Transcending all existence, it stands alone as supreme; it has endured through kalpas beyond measure without perishing.
It existed before heaven and earth, yet its beginning is unseen; it shall follow after heaven and earth, yet its end is unseen. Thus I contemplate the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
This can indeed be seen. This sutra reveals the profound essence of the Three Vehicles and unveils the primordial subtlety of the myriad dharmas.

It discourses on the emptiness that is not empty and perceives the form that is formless. It clarifies the nature of delusion, such that it may be understood through dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows;
it traces the ultimate source, such that it may be seen within the concepts of self, person, multitude, and life-span. Truly, it is the secret transmission of the Buddhas’ minds.
This is the fundamental principle for elucidating the Way of the Mahāyāna, and the pivotal mechanism by which all sentient beings clarify the mind and perceive its nature.
Now, the source of the single mind is inherently pure from the beginning. Yet, as the mind follows after objects, deluded thoughts arise;

it is like clouds rising in the vast void, suddenly forming obstructions, or like a precious mirror covered in dust, gradually losing its radiance. Consequently, by pursuing conditions, one falls into illusion. How can this be?
One is able to turn back from delusion to return to the truth. Only the Tathāgata, through his unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, has given rise to great compassion and supreme vows;

pitying the mundane world’s immersion in delusion and mindful of sentient beings’ darkness and ignorance, he has preached this sutra to extensively open up skillful means, enabling all to untangle their adhesions and release their bonds, to cleanse all defilements and depart from the dust of the world, thereby emerging from the path of birth and death and ascending to Bodhi.
It turns delusion into wisdom; it dispels darkness to reveal radiance. The merit of this sutra is vast and great. Nevertheless, the Dharma is realized through the mind;
yet there would be no way to embody the Dharma were it not for the sutra. The sutra is transmitted by people;
yet there would be no way to manifest the sutra were it not for words. Since the Tang and Song dynasties, those who have provided commentaries on this sutra have numbered in the tens of thousands.
Although the hundred schools and ten houses are numerous and their explanations are all refined through analysis, no single discourse has been able to provide a definitive synthesis.

I have long revered the Great Awakening and looked up to True Suchness (*tathatā*). Having occasionally perused various compilations, I have selected those most essential and precise passages that do not deviate from the intent of the sutras, re-editing them with great care.
I have specially ordered them to be carved into printing blocks so that they may be widely disseminated, thereby enabling the true words to penetrate deeply.
The profound meaning is brilliantly illuminated. Those who behold it are like those gazing upon the sun and moon in the midst of the sky;
those who awaken to it are like those seeking a precious jewel in the vast ocean. How joyful this is! How magnificent this is! Alas!

If virtuous people and noble scholars can indeed cultivate with diligence and sincerity, reverently worshiping and upholding [the teaching], seeking the Dharma through the sutra and attaining awakening through the Dharma, they shall immediately obtain [it].

It extinguishes immeasurable transgressions and immediately secures the attainment of the most supreme field of merit. One realizes the fruits of existence among devas and humans, forever reaching a state of happiness.
As for the extent of these meritorious virtues, how could they have any limit? I have respectfully written this preface to await future generations.
Preface dated the eighth day of the fourth month of the Gui-mao year of the Yongle era of the Ming Dynasty.
Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Diamond Sūtra:
The Greatly Awakened One among those in Heaven, the Capable Benevolent One among the sages, has opened the gate of bodhi and liberation and revealed the principle of prajñā and suchness.
He emits rays of white light from his brow that universally illuminate the oceans of lands as numerous as motes of dust; he extends his broad and long tongue...
It proclaims the supreme Mahāyāna. This Mahāyāna sūtra is truly the spiritual breast of all Buddhas and the profound treasury of all sentient beings.
It is free from names and free from marks; it is neither form nor mind. It covers heaven and earth, spanning from antiquity to the present.
In reality, its beginning cannot be reached by writing, nor can its end be reached by rolling up the scroll. To be deluded by it is to sink into oblivion for eternal kalpas; to awaken to it—
Thereupon, one is immediately liberated. Although there is a distinction between delusion and awakening, there has never been any interval between a sentient being and a Buddha.

Wherever this scripture resides, there is a Buddha present. It was His Majesty Emperor Taizong who, not forgetting the sentiments of the entrustment at Vulture Peak, conceived the intention to circulate it;
thus, he devoted his attention to the Inner Canon, scrutinizing various volumes to select those that are most refined and sublime.

To ensure that the essential purport of the scriptures was not contravened, he redoubled his efforts in compilation and specifically ordered the carving of woodblocks for printing, so as to widely disseminate them.
Thereafter, he personally applied his sagely insight and composed a preface, in which he stated:
"That which precedes heaven and earth yet shows no beginning, and follows heaven and earth yet shows no end—this can indeed be seen by observing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."
How true it is that the Honored One’s sincere words shall serve as a mirror for all eternity!

We, the disciples of the Buddha, Lai Fu and others, beholding this most supreme Mahāyāna, were as those who encounter light in darkness, as the poor who obtain treasure, as those long ill who find healing and peace, and as distant travelers returning to their native home;
we leaped for joy and, with faith and reverence, accepted and practiced its teachings. Thereupon, we gathered our like-minded companions and exhausted [our efforts].

Having relinquished precious resources, he commissioned artisans to re-carve and print this work for distribution. May it circulate far and wide; may all sentient beings of the five turbidities joyfully board the compassionate vessel of Prajñā and swiftly reach the other shore of Bodhi.

We look up with hope that the times shall be harmonious and the harvests bountiful, that rain and wind shall be favorable and regulated, and that the land shall be peaceful and the people secure, so that the Wheel of Dharma may turn forever.
Written on an auspicious day in the first ten days of the sixth month, in the third year of the Zhengtong era.
Written respectfully by Hongryeon, Right Dharma Teacher and Abbot of Nittai Kōtoku Zen-ji Temple.
The Preface to the Old Edition of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
The *Vajracchedikā* is the mind-dharma transmitted by all Buddhas, a treasury of infinite light for devas and humans.
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, when the World-Honored One held up a blue lotus flower and smiled, Kāśyapa (pronounced She) already understood this great matter.
At that time, there was no sutra of the Buddha, nor was there any preaching of a sutra. Yet, while the Dharma has neither sudden nor gradual aspects, people possess either sharp or dull faculties;
while the nature [of reality] admits neither increase nor decrease, there are superior and inferior vehicles. It is through these means that one sees, hears, perceives, and knows.

From this point on, discursive theories regarding words and letters flourished in confusion. By the time of the Tang dynasty, there were already over eight hundred schools of commentary and sub-commentary.
The true nature of the mind became obscured through mere oral transmission, bringing calamity upon successive generations; nothing could have been more extreme than this.
I humbly submit that when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they do not depart from self-nature (*svabhāva*). One must know that all phenomena arise as the functional manifestation of self-nature.

When the mind-ground is free from wrongdoing, it is the precept of self-nature; when the mind-ground is free from delusion, it is the wisdom of self-nature; when the mind-ground is free from distraction, it is the concentration of self-nature.
Constantly perceiving the self-nature of one’s own mind, practicing and liberating oneself—attaining this not through others—is precisely [the path].
Śākyamuni is one’s own nature; Maitreya is one’s own mind. It existed before heaven and earth without beginning, and it will exist after heaven and earth without end.
Thus, the One-Night Awakened One said: "The Dharmakāya is fully awakened and free of a single thing; the original source is the self-nature, the true and heavenly Buddha.
The Mountain Valley Man (Xuedou) also said: "If you knew the original source, even the Buddha would not be like him. This, furthermore—

"At the top of the hundred-foot pole" is a step forward; it is where one sets down their footing. For while nature (*xing*) is without birth or death, vital energy (*qi*) has gathering and dispersing.

When one refines the energy until it merges with nature, then the myriad sages share the same source and the ten thousand spirits are ever-present. This is what the sutras refer to as the "indestructible diamond body";
it is the ultimate achievement of studying the Buddha-way. From the very beginning, it does not depend on anything external. One must strictly avoid following the footsteps of others.
He followed [the crowd] like a calf following its mother. He once claimed that the Buddhas do not undergo saṃsāra and that sages and worthies do not fall into hell;

yet, having himself failed to reach the state of sagehood or Buddhahood, he merely echoed the views of others and relegated everything to non-existence. This is the way of petty men in later generations.

Those who dare to be without restraint or shame are resolute in committing evil and falter in pursuing goodness. They wander through the six sense-objects and are fettered by the four marks [of existence].
Deep as the surging waves of the river of craving and bitter as the drowning in the sea of desire, their physical forms remain unchanged while their conduct is worse than that of tigers and wolves;
their spirits have not yet descended into the underworld, yet their souls are already submerged among ghosts and demons. Thus one comes to know the Creator’s...
There is no creator; rather, it is the self-creation of the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence (as seen in the third section, "The Causes of Creation Depend on the Mind," etc.).

Our Buddha, the Great Compassionate One, explains through both horizontal and vertical teachings, with infinite resonance. It is like the single moon reflected in water or the wind passing through ten thousand apertures:

whatever one listens for or grasps with the eyes, all are fully satisfied. This is nothing more than to untie the adhesions and release the bonds of sentient beings, sweeping away delusions and illusions to reveal the reality.
Manifest before you: it is your original face, wherein not a single sentient being exists to be saved. Nevertheless, the Way is fundamentally wordless;
to speak of it is to coarsen it. Zen is fundamentally unspeakable; to explain it is to reduce it to the secondary.

This is why Deshan’s staff (he struck him as soon as he entered the gate) and Linji’s shout (he shouted as soon as he entered the gate), and Dayu’s three punches (Linji asked Huangbo for the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times, and on each occasion he was...)

He struck him. Later, he was enlightened by Dayu’s pointing it out. Suddenly, he attained great awakening and involuntarily cried out, "So, Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much after all! Dayu said, "What have you seen that you speak thus? Linji then delivered three punches to Dayu’s ribs.

Dayu pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo; this has nothing to do with me. Tianlong’s Single Finger: When Master Juzhi wished to travel to various places to seek the Dharma, Master Tianlong held up one finger to instruct him.
Juzhi attained enlightenment on the spot. He would often say, "I obtained Tianlong’s 'one-finger Zen'; I shall never exhaust its use throughout my life. He transmitted the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.

No words. (In the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, when Mañjuśrī asks Vimalakīrti, "We have each spoken; you, O Benevolent One, should now speak: what is the bodhisattva’s entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality?
At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word. As soon as the critical phrase is raised: "Have some tea first" (Master Zhaozhou).
It cannot be so; it cannot be not so; it cannot be both so and not so. (The Patriarchs said this, yet later venerable masters have expounded it in various ways. Arriving here, it hangs suspended.

"Letting go at the precipice; both mouth and ears are lost. As soon as there is something valued, it immediately becomes a stagnant nest. (Yantou addressed the assembly: "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere.
(The Sixth Patriarch attained enlightenment through this phrase. For that which is valued and that upon which one dwells are both considered illnesses of Chan.
They are what all Buddhas and patriarchs have condemned. When you understand such established cases as these, they are lively and vibrant; when you do not understand them...
When one attains [it], one can only play with the spirit; for a good thing is not as good as having none at all. (Attendant Wenyuan prostrated himself and was struck with a staff by Zhaozhou.)
Yuan said, "Even bowing in prostration is a good thing. Zhou said, "A good thing is not as good as having none at all.

Some say that our Way was revealed in its secrets by the masters of Liangxi and Heluo, and its completion was achieved by the two masters Zhu Xi and Zhang Zai. Their teachings are like the sun and moon; it is only that people are ill if they do not follow them.
You have studied these for many years, practicing the preservation and cultivation of the mind and the examination of one's thoughts. Now, you suddenly seek to rebel against them yourself.
[The opponent] says: "This establishes a precedent for heterodox schools and commits an offense against what is not right in the world. Why is this so? I replied:
"This single volume of scripture is held, received, recited, and contemplated by every man and woman, even in remote villages and narrow alleys.

Yet when one probes its principles and meanings, they remain utterly bewildered and do not know where it leads. Now, I have gathered the finest essence of various commentaries and followed their respective directions."
Thus, he guides them accordingly, so that every person may come to know the conduct of the Buddha. This also embodies the meaning of awakening together with others rather than awakening alone.
The Master Liu of Yuancheng once said: "Even the words of commoners gathering firewood are selected by the sages.
Now, how could the Buddha-dharma fail to include even the words of such commoners? The Master then cited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which says: "Or if they encounter..."

In the suffering of royal punishment, when facing execution at the end of one’s life, if one calls to mind the power of that Avalokiteśvara, the blade will immediately break into pieces, like slicing through water or blowing on a flame.
The natures of water and fire do not waver; it is also like swallowing various poisons—the nature of the self remains serene.
This is precisely obtaining the power of fearlessness from Avalokiteśvara. I say: if you penetrate to the realm of fearlessness, then...
Birth and death, and nirvana, are like flowers in the sky; gaining a horse or losing a sheep—none are anything other than dreams and illusions.

The three realms and the nine dark hells are all pure lands (the realms of the Three Clarities and the prisons of the Nine Darknesses); jade delicacies and coarse rice are equally a single meal; mountain forests and the morning markets are one and the same.

Wandering everywhere according to conditions, whether in adversity or prosperity, all is a land of bliss. When the mind accords with *prajñā*, what gathering or dispersing can there be for the six sense-faculties and the four great elements?
When the body accords with true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), what suffering or joy can there be when it is cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance?

(Lord Wang Jinggong, moved upon reading the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, wrote a poem: "The body is like foam or like wind; being cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, all is one emptiness. Sitting serenely in the world, one contemplates this principle; though Vimalakīrti was ill, he possessed the divine.")
This is what the Confucians call "finding self-satisfaction in whatever one enters," and what the Buddhists call "conforming to the nature of awakening.
Furthermore, those who were renowned for their mastery of Buddhist learning during the early years of the dynasty are too numerous to mention; such as the Duke Wenzheng and the Yuanwen of Meng.
Duke Yang Wen-zhuang, Duke Wen, and the recent Ch’en Chung-su and Li Chung-ting all supported the imperial axis and opened the way for a great peace;

they sustained the precarious and rescued the fallen, repelling the treacherous and expelling the heterodox, their integrity and moral fortitude so formidable that they vied with the sun for brilliance.
Yet how could this detract from the Way of Confucius? In the various works of Duke Wen-yüan, such as *Fazang Suijin*, there is nothing but the opening of the Buddha-mind.

I have observed that whenever Minister Wen Zhuang washed his face and rinsed his mouth at the fifth watch of the night, he would recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* without ceasing for thirty years.
Minister Wen associated with Chan Master Lian, from whom he derived his insights; he then compiled the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) to edify future generations.
Viewed from this perspective, one cannot judge a person based merely on their outward traces. Some say: "When Deshan carried..."
*Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra*. While traveling south, he visited Longtan. At night, he entered the room;

as he drew back the curtain and stepped out, Longtan lit a paper candle and handed it to him. Just as Deshan was about to accept it, Longtan blew it out. At that moment, Deshan attained great enlightenment and immediately burned his commentary to ashes. (Deshan had long been occupied with the *Diamond Sūtra*.

Later, hearing that the Chan school was flourishing in the south, he took his commentaries and traveled south. He first arrived at Longtan. When night fell, he entered the room and stood in attendance until late. Longtan said, "Why do you not leave? Deshan then drew back the curtain and went out. Longtan then...)

As he was lighting a paper candle to hand it over, Master Shan took up his notes and commentaries in front of the Dharma Hall, held up a torch, and said: "To exhaust all fundamental arguments is like placing a single hair in the vast void;

to exhaust all worldly mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a great abyss. He then burned the notes and commentaries. [The opponent] says: "Now you are merely picking up the trap and the snare;

this is truly what is called 'spending a hundred years drilling through old paper—there will never be a time of emerging. " He replied: "If you want to reach mastery, you must strike from right here."
[This is] an error. It is as if, before having even attained the stage of a virtuous mountain-dweller, one wishes to burn the commentaries.

I fear deeply that you have not yet dreamed of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. One day, I mentioned this to Pan Shunqing and Gong Dezhuang, who laughed heartily (*da xiao*) and said, "Only Shunqing is a man of pure cultivation from the Zai-chu era;
he abstains from meat and wine and is profoundly learned in this sūtra. We should compile [the work] together."
The merit of this undertaking is especially great. Yang Gui, having contributed his gold, had the woodblocks carved to broaden the gift of the Dharma.

I respectfully invoke the Eight Vajras (the *Tattvārthā-ṭīkā* states: "There are six kinds of Vajras; when facing the practitioner of the Sūtra, one attains untainted merit through practice. As for why they are here called 'eight,' it is because they face the practitioner.")
Transforming the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms;
I respectfully invoke the Vajra of Blue Disaster-Dispelling (the lord who dispels the calamities and misfortunes of all sentient beings from past lives and presides over the great ocean);
I respectfully invoke the Vajra of Dispelling Poison (the lord who dispels the pestilence and toxic ailments of all sentient beings and presides over calamitous poisons).
I respectfully invoke the Yellow Sāravidyāvajra (the Lord of Merit who causes all sentient beings to have their aspirations fulfilled as they wish).
I respectfully invoke the White Vimalodakavajra (the Lord of All Jewels who removes the suffering of feverish affliction for all sentient beings).
I respectfully invoke the Red Ghoṣāgnivajra (the Lord who causes all sentient beings to clearly perceive the Buddhas through the ninefold vision and gives rise to the wind-energy).
I reverently invoke the Vajra Who Holds Stability Against Calamities (the Lord of Lapis Lazuli who removes the misfortunes and sufferings of all sentient beings);
I reverently invoke the Vajra Purple Sage (the Lord of the Firm Treasury who enables the hearts of all sentient beings to open and attain awakening);
I reverently invoke the Great Deity Vajra (the Lord of the Dragon Kings who causes the sprouts of wisdom to flourish in all sentient beings).
I respectfully invoke the four bodhisattvas (who are the four immeasurable minds):
I respectfully invoke the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi (Maitrī);
I respectfully invoke the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa (Karuṇā).

In the *Jingang banruo boluomi jing Xianyoweng ji*, Ying says:
"Vajra" refers to that which is the most refined and solid among gold; it is produced from within gold.
It cannot be melted even after a hundred refinements. Taking this hardness and sharpness, it can sever and destroy all things.
Although all five metals are called "gold," when one speaks of "gold" in common parlance, it refers to iron. This term "vajra" (diamond/thunderbolt) is like the steel used for swords and blades.
For example, wisdom can sever greed, anger, ignorance, and all inverted views. *Prajñāpāramitā*...

"Jie" (若) is the Sanskrit term (Sanskrit being the language of the West). "Zhihui" (智慧) is the Chinese term (Chinese being the language of China). Its essential nature is empty and harmonious, and its illumination and function are sovereign;
therefore, it is called *prajñā*. The Sanskrit term *pāramitā* is translated in Chinese as "reaching the other shore."

To reach the other shore, one must rely upon Prajñā (wisdom). This shore refers to the realm where sentient beings perform karma, undergo suffering, and transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death.
The other shore refers to the realm of ultimate liberation, purity, and peace attained by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Ordinary beings are this shore; the Buddha-way is the other shore. A single thought of evil—this is...

This shore. A single thought of goodness is itself the other shore. The six realms of existence—(the six realms being devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals)—are like a sea of suffering.
There is no boat by which one does not cross; take the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) as the vessel (note: *du* is synonymous with *du*; the six perfections will be explained in detail later).

Wang Rihui said: "The Sanskrit word *a* means 'non-'; the Sanskrit word *nuttara* means 'supreme';
the Sanskrit word *samyak* means 'right'; the Sanskrit word *sambodhi* means 'perfectly equal. The Sanskrit word *bodhi* means 'awakening.
Thus, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the Unsurpassed, Right, Perfect, and Complete Awakening."
This refers to the true nature (*tathatā*). The true nature is itself the Buddha. In Sanskrit, "Buddha" means "Awakened" (*buddha*); thus, to speak briefly, one calls it "Awakening.
To speak in detail, one calls it "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Awakening" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Because this true nature cannot be attained and is beyond all that is superior, it is called "unsurpassed. Yet, from the Buddhas above down to the most minute insects below, [all possess it].

This nature is perfectly equal in its true characteristics; hence it is called "Perfect Equality" (Samyak-saṃbodhi). Its awakening is perfect, luminous, and universally illuminating, being without partiality or deficiency;
hence it is called "Perfect Awakening" (Samyak-saṃbuddha). One who attains this nature is therefore a Buddha, and thereby transcends and is liberated from the three realms.
"One shall no longer transmigrate.
Sengruo Na said: "When Bodhisattvas first begin their practice, they all give rise to this vast and great mind.

Wang Rihui said: "Ying" means "should. "Yun" means "to say. "Yunhe" (how) means "in what manner.

Subhūti here asks the Buddha: "If a good man or a good woman should give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—that is, the mind that seeks true nature to achieve Buddhahood—and having given rise to this seeking of true nature..."
Regarding the mind that seeks to attain Buddhahood: how should it abide? This means: in what state should it dwell?
How should one subdue this mind? This means: how should one subdue this deluded mind?
The monk Ruone said: "Subhūti has precisely raised these two questions:

first, regarding sentient beings who resolve to seek prajñā with a mind free from [attachment to] lands, how can they abide securely in the principle of truth? Second, regarding the subduing of the deluded mind."
How can one subdue and gather back the scattered mind? What is taught in the sutras does not go beyond this subduing and settling.
Li Wenhui said: "What is meant by 'subduing the mind'? Subhūti refers to the deluded thoughts of ordinary beings."
“Afflictions are boundless. By relying on what dharma can they be subdued?
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.”

Li Wenhui said: "What you have said is the Buddha praising Subhūti for being able to understand my intention, skillfully instructing all people not to give rise to deluded thoughts, but to keep the mind constantly diligent so as not to become stained by or attached to the characteristics of dharmas.
Regarding 'listen attentively': 'attentive' (di) means 'to comprehend. You should thoroughly comprehend that the sensory object of sound is fundamentally unborn."
"Do not pursue the words; listen with careful examination.

[He] dwells. Thus he subdues his mind. [He] remains silent. "World-Honored One, I wish and desire to hear."

Li Wenhui said: "As for 'should abide thus,' it means that when the Tathāgata desires to cause the minds of sentient beings to be neither arising nor ceasing, but rather profoundly still and pure, they will then be able to see their nature."
Master Pang said: "The people of the world prize precious jewels, but I cherish a moment of stillness. Abundant gold disturbs the human mind;
through stillness, one perceives the nature of True Suchness.
Master Xiaoyao said: "The minds of ordinary beings are active and deluded; the minds of sages are still and luminous. Furthermore:

It is said: "When the mind and environment of ordinary people are pure, this is the Buddha’s Pure Land; when the mind and environment are turbid and chaotic, this is the defiled land of the Mara King.
Master Huangbo said: "Ordinary beings are mostly obstructed by objects within their minds, and by phenomena within their principles; they constantly desire to flee from these objects."
Settle the mind. When affairs are screened away by means of principle, one does not realize that this is actually the mind obstructing the environment and principle obstructing affairs.
Simply cause the mind to be empty and the environment will naturally be empty; cause the mind to be quiescent and affairs will naturally be quiescent.

Do not apply the mind perversely. It is further said: "Ordinary people grasp at objects; the wise grasp at the mind. The simultaneous disappearance of both mind and object is the true Dharma. It is still easier to eliminate objects."
To lose the mind is extremely difficult. People do not dare to lose their minds, fearing they will fall into emptiness where there is no place to grasp or seek.

They do not know that emptiness is fundamentally empty and is nothing other than the single true Dharma-realm. Ordinary people all give rise to thoughts by pursuing external objects, thereby producing likes and dislikes.
If one wishes to eliminate external objects, one must lose the mind. When the mind is lost, objects become empty; when objects are empty, the mind [is lost].
[The mind] is extinguished. If one does not eliminate the mind but merely attempts to remove objects, objects cannot be removed; it only serves to increase confusion and turmoil.
Therefore, while the myriad dharmas are but the mind, the mind itself is unattainable. Since nothing can be attained, this is the ultimate state. Why needlessly strive further for liberation?
One who subdues the mind in this manner, upon seeing their own nature, will find that there is nothing [to be attained].
"Delusive thoughts. Since there are no delusive thoughts, this is precisely what it means to subdue the mind. "Only" (wei) is a word used for assent;
"indeed" (ran) refers to fulfilling one's expectations. "Willingly and joyfully desiring to hear" means to delight in and wish to hear that Dharma.
Chen Xiong said: “‘Wei’ means to assent to those words; ‘ran’ means that those words are indeed so. Yan Bing said:
“To give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—in the language of Tang, this refers to the mind of supreme, perfect, and equal enlightenment—is what is meant by ‘should.
To ‘abide’ means to dwell eternally without ceasing. Xu... [text ends]
Bodhi asked: "For those sons and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain bodhicitta, how should they abide so as to remain eternally and without extinction?
How can they subdue their minds? The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! These are words of praise.
Those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta should abide in this way, should subdue their minds in this way, and should act in this way.
"Zhe" (this) means precisely this very thing. "Wei ran" (so be it) is Subhūti’s expression of assent, no different from Zengzi’s saying "Wei" (yes).
"Le" (joy/delight) means love; he wishes with love to hear the preaching of the Dharma.
Chan Master Zhizhe composed a verse, saying: "How rare, how rare is the Buddha! The wondrous principle reaches the ultimate nirvāṇa. (As the *Yilan ji*, in the "Chapter on Entering Nirvāṇa," states:
'When his tasks are finished, the person enters nirvāṇa; the śarīra remains to perform the Buddha-work. How can he dwell in subduing? To dwell in subduing is difficult.

The wondrousness within the laws of the two polarities— Master Fu said: 'The principle of the Dharma-body is like the great void. Vertically it exhausts the three periods of time; horizontally it spans the ten directions. It encompasses the eight extremities and includes all things.'"

The Two Principles (*dvy-āyatanas*). What is meant by "encompassing the Two Principles" is identical in meaning to the subtle intent within these two principles of the Dharma. The teachings and metaphors of the Three Vehicles are broad:

(In the three fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Buddha says that by relying on these Three Vehicles, one shall obtain happiness and seek one's own nirvāṇa; this is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle. Delighting in solitary tranquility is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
Delivering and liberating all beings is called the Mahāyāna. Excellent! Now listen attentively; the six thieves will be spared from obstruction.
Section Three: The Orthodox Tradition of the Mahāyāna.

The Mahāyāna is not the Hīnayāna; the orthodox tradition is not a heterodox tradition (*The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* states: "Vehicle" has the meaning of practice. Wang Rixiu says: "Vehicle" refers to a carriage).
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner.
Li Wenhui said: "Mahāsattva—'mahā' means great. Their mental capacity is vast and expansive, immeasurable;
they are truly people of great enlightenment."
The King’s explanation is detailed in the second fascicle.
Regarding "all classes of sentient beings" (the *Lotus Sūtra* reads this with the level tone).
The Sixth Patriarch said: "All" is a general designation; what follows below is a specific enumeration of nine types.
King Rihui said: "All those who have birth are called *sattvas* (sentient beings). From the heavens above down to the most minute insects, none escape having birth;
therefore, they are called 'all sentient beings. Although sentient beings are countless and infinite, they do not exceed nine types, as described in the following text."

Li Wenhui said: "Sentient beings" refers to those who, regarding all things—whether good or evil, ordinary or sage—possess a mind of grasping and rejecting, giving rise to immeasurable and boundless afflictions and delusive thoughts, thereby transmigrating through the six realms of existence.
Sengruo Ne said: "The term 'sentient beings' (zhòngshēng) should be pronounced with the departing tone (qùshēng), yet nowadays it is all pronounced with the level tone (píngshēng).
This has been handed down from antiquity for the sake of convenience in address."
Whether born from eggs, born from a womb, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless;
whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing perception nor lacking perception.

The Sixth Patriarch said: "Those born from eggs are those whose nature is deluded. Those born from wombs are those whose nature is habituated. Those born from moisture are those whose nature follows what is heterodox.
Those born by transformation are those whose nature pursues views. Because of delusion, one creates various karmas; because of habituation, one constantly transmigrates;

because of following what is heterodox, the mind is unsettled; because of pursuing views, one falls into the Avīci (pronounced *ping sheng*) hell. To give rise to thoughts and cultivate the mind is itself a false view."

No. Not internally harmonizing with the principle of formlessness is called "having form. Keeping the inner mind upright while failing to practice reverence and making offerings—merely claiming that a straightforward mind is the Buddha and failing to cultivate merit and wisdom—is called "formless.

Failing to understand the Middle Way, yet seeing with the eyes, hearing with the ears, contemplating with the mind, and becoming attached to the marks of phenomena while speaking of the Buddha’s conduct with the mouth... the mind...

Not relying on practice is called "having thought" (*saṃjñā*). Deluded people practicing *dhyāna* single-mindedly eliminate delusions, yet do not study compassion, joy, equanimity, wisdom, or skillful means;
they are like wood or stone, devoid of function, and are thus called "without thought" (*asaṃjñā*).

Because they do not cling to the perceptions of these two dharmas, it is called "neither having thought"; because the mind seeking the principle remains present, it is called "neither without thought."
Wang Rihui said: "As for those born from eggs, these range from the large, such as the garuḍa, to the minute, such as lice and nits.
As for those born from wombs, these range from the large, such as lions and elephants, to the medium, such as humans, to the small, such as cats and mice."
Those born from moisture are such as fish, turtles, crocodiles, and soft-shelled turtles, down to the most minute insects within water.

Those born by transformation include those above, such as devas; those below, such as those in the hells; and those in between, such as humans, as well as all the insects produced within rice, wheat, fruits, and the like.
These four aforementioned types refer to sentient beings of the desire realm. If there are...
Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): form refers to the physical body (*rūpakāya*). This refers to the various devas from the first dhyāna heaven up to the fourth dhyāna heaven;
they possess only a physical body and lack the forms of male and female, as their sensual desires have already been severed. This is what is called the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
As for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this refers to the devas of the formless realm. These are situated above the fourth dhyāna heaven.
There is only the conscious spirit (vijñāna) and no physical body; therefore, it is called the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
If there is perception (saṃjñā), these are referred to as the gods of the Heaven of Perception (saṃjñā-deva). These celestial beings possess only mental ideation; hence, from this point upward—

All these are called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), for they no longer possess a physical body. As for those who are "without perception" (*asaṃjñin*), this refers to the gods of the Heaven of No-Perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).

They reside above the Heaven of Perception (*saṃjñideva*). Because these celestial beings remain in a state of singular stillness and immobility for a single moment of thought, it is named the Heaven of No-Perception.
As for those who are "neither with perception nor without perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñin*), this refers to the... [text fragment ends]
These are the devas of the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). This heaven is situated above the Heaven of No Perception (*asaṃjñāyatana*).
Because the beings of this heaven remain in a state of singular stillness and immobility for a single moment of thought, it is called "not having perception" (*na saṃjñā*).

Yet, because they do not resemble wood or stone and are thus incapable of being entirely without perception, it is called "not without perception" (*nāsaṃjñā*). Among all the heavens within the three realms (*tridhātu*), this heaven is the highest.
Their lifespan is extremely long, not limited to merely eighty thousand kalpas.
Li Wenhui said: "As for those born from eggs, they are greedily attached to ignorance, enveloped by delusion and darkness.

As for those born from wombs, because external objects come into contact with them, they subsequently give rise to deviant thoughts. As for those born from moisture, as soon as an evil thought arises..."
One immediately falls into the three miserable realms; that is to say, greed, anger, and delusion are obtained through these causes.

As for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), all afflictions are fundamentally rootless; they suddenly exist due to the arising of a mind of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, a sutra in the teachings states:
"All sentient beings are fundamentally complete [in nature], yet they receive retribution according to their karma; therefore, ignorance constitutes birth from an egg."

Enveloped by afflictions (*kleśa*), one is born from a womb; drenched by the waters of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one is born from moisture; and arising suddenly through afflictions, one is born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Furthermore, it is said that when the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue fail to turn their light inward to illuminate, there is that which is greedily leaked out.
One then falls into the four modes of birth—namely, those born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation.

When the light of the senses turns inward to illuminate within, so that there is no longer any craving or outflow regarding forms, sounds, smells, or tastes, one realizes the four fruits of spiritual attainment—namely, the stage of Srotāpanna and the others.

Master Fu said: "When Śūnyatāputra first posed his question, the Sugata responded according to the capacity of the seeker. First he answered how one should dwell; next he taught how one should practice.
Beings born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation—all are to be gathered in by compassion and wisdom.

If one gives rise to the view of a sentient being, it is no different from seeking through attachment to signs. 'If there is form' refers to the mind of ordinary people who cling to existence and perceive falsely."
This is not in accord with the principle of signlessness (*animitta*). If one is without form, one clings to the mark of emptiness and fails to cultivate merit and wisdom.

If one possesses conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), then upon seeing with the eyes or hearing with the ears, one gives rise to false imaginings; though the mouth speaks of the Buddha’s conduct, the mind does not rely upon that conduct.
If one is without conceptualization, one sits in meditation to eliminate delusions, becoming like wood or stone, and thus fails to practice compassion and wisdom.

Regarding the skillful means of wisdom (*prajñā-upāya*): if one does not possess right perception, the sūtras within the teachings state that both existence and non-existence are discarded, and both speech and silence are forgotten.
To have a mind of grasping and rejecting, or of hatred and love, is to fail to understand the Middle Way. Master Linji said:
"Entering the mundane and entering the sacred, entering defilement and entering purity—appearing in all lands everywhere—all are nothing but the empty characteristic of all phenomena."
This is called the authentic and correct view. If you love the holy and hate the ordinary, you will continue to float and sink within the ocean of birth and death.
"Not being without thought" means that there is still a mind seeking the principle.
"I shall cause all of them to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and bring them to liberation.
Li Wenhui said: "I" refers to the Buddha speaking of himself. "All" means collectively. "Cause" means to direct. "Enter" means to awaken and enter.
"Without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) refers to true permanence and profound stillness. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The Buddha shall act for..."
To sever and exhaust them until nothing remains is *nirvāṇa*. In this regard, the Bodhisattva’s mind is free from grasping or rejecting;

it is like the great orb of the moon—perfectly full and tranquil. Sentient beings are deluded regarding the signless dharma of *nirvāṇa*, and thus they take on the conditioned bodies of birth and death.
"Extinction" (*mie*) means to eliminate and extinguish; "deliverance" (*du*) means to transform and deliver.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "The Tathāgata pointed out that within the three realms and nine stages, each possesses the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, commanding one to awaken to and enter it for oneself.
'Without remainder' means being free from residual habit-energies and afflictions. 'Nirvāṇa' carries the meaning of perfect purity;
only when all habit-energies are extinguished so they no longer arise does one accord with this. 'To deliver' means to cross over birth and death."

It is like the great ocean. The Buddha’s mind is impartial; he universally vows that all sentient beings shall together enter the perfect, pure, and signless nirvana, together cross the great ocean of birth and death, and together realize what all Buddhas have realized.

Though afflictions are of ten thousand variations, they are all but the defiled mind; though physical forms are innumerable, they are collectively called "sentient beings. Thus, the Tathāgata’s great compassion is universal.
[He] transformed [them], causing them all to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. The *Song of Realizing the Way* says: "Those who have attained [realization] travel together on the path of *nirvāṇa*.
The commentary states: "*Nirvāṇa* means neither arising nor ceasing. 'Nie' (Nir) means not arising; 'pan' (vāṇa) means not ceasing. This is the path of non-arising.
Chongying Zhenren Zhou Shiqing responded to the monk Chibutuo.
Pointing to the incense smoke, he said: "If you wish to contemplate the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder) of a student, the ashes in the incense burner are it.
If you wish to contemplate the *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) of a student, the ashes in the incense burner having completely vanished are it."
Wang Rihui said: "The Sanskrit term *nirvāṇa* is translated here as 'unconditioned' (*wuwei*).
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that *nirvāṇa* is the realm of purity, neither dying nor being born, the refuge and destination for all practitioners.
Thus, *nirvāṇa* is the ground of transcending saṃsāra and departing from birth and death; it is truly most supreme and wondrous."
This is not what is meant by death. People of the world do not understand this principle and mistakenly take it to be death; this is a great error.
This nirvana without remainder is itself the Great Nirvana. Because there is nothing else remaining beyond this nirvana, it is called "nirvana without remainder.
This refers to the aforementioned exhaustion of all that exists within the worlds.
The nine classes of sentient beings are all transformed so that they attain Buddhahood and achieve the nirvana of a Buddha.
In this way, although immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings are brought to extinction, in reality, there are no sentient beings who have attained extinction.
Wang Rihui said: "All sentient beings manifest from within their own karmic conditions. Thus, those with the karmic conditions for being human are born as humans;
those who have cultivated the karmic conditions for the heavens are born in the heavens;
those who have created the karmic conditions for animals are born as animals; and those who have fashioned the causes and conditions for hell are born in hell."
Regarding the hells: as with the nine classes of sentient beings mentioned above, there is not one who is not born through the conditions of their own karma.
Originally, these sentient beings do not exist. Therefore, the Bodhisattva resolves to transform them, causing them all to attain Buddhahood and enter nirvāṇa;
yet in reality, not a single sentient being is brought to nirvāṇa, because originally no sentient beings exist.
Sengruo Ne said: "Within the primary principle (paramārtha), there is no birth that can be saved; this is precisely the eternal mind.
If one perceives that there is something to be saved, this is birth-and-death. This is truly because all sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas;
what birth is there to be saved? This is what is called the equal and true Dharma-realm: 'The Buddha does not save sentient beings.'"
Chen Xiong said: "The wisdom of the Mahāyāna is inherently possessed by all. Yet sentient beings are unable to awaken to it on their own;

it is the Buddha who truly awakens them, causing immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to extinguish within their own minds all ignorance, false views, and afflictions—bringing them all to *parinirvāṇa*.
Though those brought to *parinirvāṇa* are so numerous, he further says that in truth there are none."

As for those sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa, it is ultimately attributed to the sentient beings themselves; they deliver themselves through their own inherent nature. What merit do I possess? The *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* states:
"To deliver oneself through one's own inherent nature is called true deliverance. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "The fundamental nature of all sentient beings is eternally extinguished;
it does not undergo further extinction. When Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked the World-Honored One, [the Buddha replied that] in reality there are none...
"How is it that sentient beings attain extinction? The World-Honored One replied, "Their nature is fundamentally pure;
being without birth and without extinction, there are no sentient beings who attain extinction, nor is there any nirvana to be reached. All these simply return to the self-nature of sentient beings.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "If a person wishes to thoroughly know all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the Dharma..."
The nature of the realms: all are created solely by the mind. A verse on the mind as the cause of transformation states: "The assignment of forms each arises from the mind;
like shadows and echoes, there is no deception. Originally, there is no creative power; it is the myriad beings themselves who transform."
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, then he is not a bodhisattva.
(In the Goryeo edition, the name of the patriarch is Jik; to avoid taboo characters, "Ji" was changed to "Ce.")

The Sixth Patriarch said: "Practitioners also possess four marks. To have a mind that distinguishes between subject and object, and to treat sentient beings with contempt, is called the mark of self (ātman).

To rely on one's own observance of the precepts and look down upon those who break them is called the mark of person (pudgala). To loathe the sufferings of the three miserable realms and vow to be reborn among the devas is the mark of sentient beings (sattva).
To cherish long life and diligently cultivate meritorious deeds while failing to forget attachment to dharmas is the mark of phenomena (dharma)."
This is the mark of a self-possessor (*jīva*). There are four marks; these are sentient beings. To be without the four marks is to be a Buddha. Sengruo said:
"As for the term 'mark of self' (*ātman*), it refers to the six consciousnesses of one's own mind continuing without interruption.
To grasp at a self within this is the view that calculates the internal. The 'mark of a person' (*pudgala*) refers to the external objects of the six realms, which are collectively termed..."
Regarding these various objects, the person (pudgala) clings to each one individually, discriminating between superior and inferior, and asserting "that exists" and "this exists.
Because this view is established based on external phenomena, it is called the mark of the person (*pudgalanimitta*).

As for the mark of the sentient being (*sattvanimitta*), it refers to the initial entry of the preceding consciousness-mind into the parents' union, followed by the continuity of the four aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and formations; the reckoning of this combination is termed a "sentient being."
Regarding the mark of a "life-span possessor" (*jīvaka-nimitta*): it refers to calculating that one's life-force (*jīvitendriya*) will remain uninterrupted for the duration of this single lifetime;

hence it is called the mark of a life-span possessor. Chen Xiong said: Greed, anger, delusion, and craving constitute the four evil karmas. Greed involves making private calculations for oneself, which constitutes the mark of a self (*ātma-nimitta*).
Anger involves discriminating between "you" and "I," which constitutes the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*). Delusion involves being stubborn, arrogant, and insolent, which is...
Regarding the mark of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*): to cherish and long for longevity is the mark of a self (*ātmagrāha*).

The Tathāgata does not regard the deliverance of sentient beings as a merit, for he realizes there is nothing to be attained; this is because he has completely eliminated these four marks. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:
"If one has not yet eliminated the four marks, one cannot achieve Bodhi. Thus, the Bodhisattva sets forth upon the unsurpassed path of Bodhi.
The mind receives the Tathāgata’s teaching on signlessness; how could there be four kinds of signs?
If even one such sign were present, one would necessarily give rise to the thought of being able to deliver sentient beings. This is the view of a sentient being, not that of a Bodhisattva.
A Bodhisattva and a sentient being originally possess no different natures: when awakened, sentient beings are Bodhisattvas; when deluded, [Bodhisattvas are sentient beings].
Bodhisattvas are sentient beings; they possess these four kinds of characteristics. Whether they are deluded or awakened depends entirely upon them.
As for the phrase "Why is this so?", it is a term used for dialectical discussion.

The Buddha, fearing that the various bodhisattvas might not understand the teaching of true emptiness and signlessness, engaged in such discussion and thus addressed these four kinds of characteristics. (Chapter Seventeen, Section Twenty-five)
The various commentaries all state:
Yan Bing said, "Regarding 'all sentient beings,' the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: those who see the Buddha-nature are not called sentient beings;
those who do not see the Buddha-nature are called sentient beings. *Mahā* means 'great. The Buddha told Subhūti..."

Regarding those who speak of the Great Awakened Nature: whether they be born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or by transformation; whether they be wriggling, crawling, or sentient beings; whether they possess form or lack form;
whether they have the perception of being sentient or the perception of being insentient; and even those that do not belong to the two realms of existence or non-existence.
Although the physical bodies of sentient beings differ, their nature is each without duality.

These ten classes of sentient beings, I shall cause all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation. As for *nirvāṇa*: "non-arising" is called *ni*, and "non-dying" is called *vāṇa*.
The Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata realizes *nirvāṇa*, eternally severing birth and death. 'Extinction' (*nirodha*) means the total extinction of all afflictions;
'deliverance' (*mokṣa*) means being liberated from the ocean of suffering that is birth and death. 'To cause' (*yō*) means to lead. 'I shall cause them all to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
'Without remainder' (*anupadhiśeṣa*) means that although an Arhat realizes *nirvāṇa*, there still remains a residue of body and cognition. As it is said in the Sūtra..."
That which has a remainder is called *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; only when body and wisdom remain as a residue is it called *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, it is said:
"In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. Once sentient beings have realized that their fundamental nature is empty and quiescent, what further is there to be extinguished?
If the four marks of existence cannot be suddenly and directly emptied, then one is not the awakened nature of a bodhisattva.
Li Wenhui said:
"The mark of self (*ātman*) is to rely upon and take pride in one’s status, rank, power, wealth, treasures, and learning;

it is to seek out the high and connect with the noble, while treating those who are poor, lowly, ignorant, or deluded with contempt. The mark of others (*pudgala*) is to possess a mind of subject and object."

The mark of intellectual understanding (*jñāna*) is to claim attainment when one has not attained it, and to claim realization when one has not realized it; to rely on one's own observance of the precepts while disparaging those who break them.

The mark of the notion of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*) is to harbor a mind of covetous seeking and expectation; to speak of what is correct while practicing what is perverse, and to have a virtuous mouth but an evil heart.

The mark of the notion of a life-span (*jīvita-saṃjñā*) is to appear as if awakened during moments of awareness, yet to give rise to emotional attachment upon encountering objects and to cling to various marks while yearning for them.
If one possesses these four characteristics, one is identical to ordinary sentient beings and is not a bodhisattva.
Master Linji said: "Within the field of the five-aggregate body, there is the True Person of No Rank, manifest and revealed in full majesty."
Why do you not recognize it? Simply, at all times, never allow for interruption; it is present before your very eyes.

It is only because emotions arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because conceptualizations shift that the essence appears diverse. Thus, one transmigrates through the three realms and undergoes all manner of suffering.
I venture to ask: for all people, everything encountered by the eye is thus. What is this? Every mountain and river is without obstruction;
layer upon layer of pavilions open in response to the season.
Chan Master Chuanshan said: "Standing atop heaven and rooted in earth, with a straight nose and slanting eyes. He further composed a verse: "The grand and majestic Great Way is brilliantly manifest;
Every person is fully endowed with it, and each individual has perfected it. It is only because of a single moment of deviation That the myriad forms come into being."

Sublime practice is fundamentally without abiding or attachment.
Furthermore, Subhūti:

A bodhisattva should abide in nothing when practicing the giving of alms (the Buddha’s term "giving" corresponds to what the Confucian tradition calls "application").
The *Shuchao* states: "Regarding the phrase 'should abide in nothing': 'should' means 'ought to'; 'abiding in nothing' means that the mind does not cling."
Li Wenhui said: "Regarding 'the Bodhisattva in regard to dharmas,' this generally indicates all dharmas of both emptiness and existence.
'He should abide nowhere' means that one should not abide in or become attached to any dharmas whatsoever. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
Within the lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma, which is to say, the One Mind. The mind is itself the Dharma;
the Dharma is itself the mind. Those of the Two Vehicles cannot understand or awaken to this; they claim that apart from the mind, there exists a separate Dharma.
They give rise to contrary attachments and dwell upon the marks of phenomena; this is identical to the views of ordinary beings. Master Xiaoyao said:
