Commentary on the Diamond Sutra, Scroll Three:
Chapter Fourteen, “The Section on Detachment from Characteristics and Quiescent Extinction.
Directly and suddenly empty, one is detached from all forms and characteristics. Since one is detached from forms and characteristics, quiescent extinction manifests before one.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and said to the Buddha:
"It is rare, World-Honored One! That the Buddha should preach such a profound sutra as this.
From the past until now, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard a sutra such as this."
Chen Xiong said: "One who deeply understands the meaning and intent is Subhūti, whose mind has awakened to the principle that true emptiness is signless.
His weeping and lamentation stem from his sorrow that he encountered [the Dharma] so late, failing to achieve awakening earlier."
Yan Bing said: "Deep understanding" refers to great penetration and great awakening.

Li Wenhui said: When Subhūti heard this sutra being preached, he fully realized the emptiness of both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) and immediately attained the principle of the Middle Way.
He marveled at its rarity and, moved to the utmost degree, shed tears. "Never having heard it before" refers to the past...
Having attained the eye of wisdom, one perceives emptiness within existence; now, upon hearing this sutra, even that [perception of] emptiness is dispelled.
This is the realization of the Middle Way, intended to initiate the teaching for the sake of future generations.
Master Fu’s Verse says: Hearing the sutra, I deeply understand its meaning; my heart is filled with both joy and sorrow.
All afflictions have been eliminated, yet none can escape the cognitive obscurations. The imputed nature was realized long ago; the perfected nature is realized at this moment.
Riding upon the unimpeded wisdom of past vehicles, I employ skillful means to exhort others to uphold [the Dharma].
Master Chuanshan’s verse says: "Since my youth, I have been accustomed to distant lands; Time and again I have crossed the Xiang River at Mount Heng.
Only when I stepped upon the path home Did I realize how long the days and months had been on the road."
World-Honored One, if there should be anyone who hears this sutra and, with pure faith, gives rise to the mark of reality,
you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
Li Wenhui said: "One whose mind of faith is pure" means believing that the original mind has no dharma that can be grasped;

thus, deluded thoughts do not arise, and the mind is constantly empty and still, profoundly pure. "Thereby giving rise to the true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa) means suddenly and completely awakening to all dharmas, which are established by virtue of this pure mind;
this is called the true mark, and it achieves the foremost, rare, and sublime merit.
As for "virtue": when deluded, the Buddha is a sentient being; when awakened, the sentient being is the Buddha. The Way of all Buddhas is equal;

there is no dharma with which it can be compared. Chen Xiong said: "Within the nature is contained the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata; this is what is called the true mark of birth. *Yuanjue* (Perfect Enlightenment).
The Sūtra says: "Because all true marks (dharmatā) are pure by nature, one awakens to the principle and thereby realizes the true mark.
I know that among those who accomplish the merits of the Dharma-body, none can surpass this; thus it is called the foremost rarity.
It is indeed true that the Sūtras have repeatedly stated that merit is accompanied by virtue, yet here alone do they speak specifically of "merit and virtue" (guṇa-puṇya).
Regarding "that which does not equal merit": when the fruition of this practice is perfected and complete, then that merit becomes something unworthy of mention.
This is why the sutras specifically state that "merit and virtue" reside within the *dharmakāya*, rather than residing in merit itself.
Master Fu’s verse says: There has never been a mind without an object, nor has there ever been a mind without an object. When the object perishes, the mind naturally ceases;
when the mind ceases, the object cannot encroach. What the sutras call the "true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is a wondrous expression whose principle is profoundly deep.
Only a Buddha can realize and know this; how could lesser sages possibly bear it?
Yan Bing said: "That which is called the 'true mark' (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is precisely the awakening to one's own nature.
World-Honored One, this true mark is itself markless; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'true mark.'"
Yan Bing said: "The Buddha taught that 'true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is signless.

That which is called true reality is precisely the absence of signs, like the vast void, wherein not a single form or sign exists. If one awakens to true reality, one must not cling to it as a fixed reality.
As the Great Being [Nāgārjuna] said: 'Seeking further beyond the other shore, one speaks only of provisional names; true reality is fundamentally unobtainable.'"
Li Wenhui said: "That which is called 'non-characteristic' refers to the fact that the true characteristic is itself without characteristic;

therefore, it is described as 'non-. This does not mean that there is no true characteristic at all, like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. One merely says that the tortoise has no hair and the rabbit has no horns; one does not say that there is no tortoise-hair or rabbit-horn.
Likewise, one merely says that the true characteristic is without characteristic; one does not say that there is no true characteristic."
The Patriarch Bodhidharma said: "If you understand the true mark (dharmatā), you see that which is not a mark. If you comprehend that which is not a mark, its form is likewise so.
One should not give rise to the substance of form within form; yet within that which is not a mark, one does not obstruct existence.
It is just like the flavor of salt in water or the blue pigment in lacquer: it is certainly present, yet its shape is not seen. This—
It is said:
Master Fu Daoshi stated, "Sentient beings and the life-principle are merely empty names established upon the aggregates;
they are as unreal as a tortoise's hair and as formless as a rabbit's horns."
Chan Master Chuanshan said: "Where did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth come from? He offered this verse: "Viewing the mountains from afar, they possess color;
Listening to the waters nearby, there is no sound. The spring has passed, yet the flowers remain; People come, but the birds are not startled.
(An ancient poem on a painted screen) Every point is fully revealed; in every thing, the essence is fundamentally level. Why do you say you do not understand? It is simply because it is too clear.
“World-Honored One, for me now to hear such a sutra as this, and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, would not be difficult.
Wang Rihui said: “To ‘believe and understand’ means to trust in its meaning and comprehend it.
To ‘accept and uphold’ means to be able to receive its meaning and maintain it.”

Chen Xiong said: "To be free from doubt is called faith (śraddhā). To clearly understand the meaning is called comprehension (adhimukti). To reverently accept without neglect is called receiving (udgrahaṇa).
To wear it upon oneself without weariness is called upholding (dhāraṇā)."

Li Wenhui said: "Simply to realize the emptiness of both person and phenomena, to have a mind free from grasping or rejecting, and to constantly maintain a state of empty stillness—this is called faith, understanding, receiving, and upholding.
Through the compassionate skillful means of the Tathāgata, deluded people are transformed and guided.
When deluded, the Buddha is a sentient being; when awakened, sentient beings are the Buddha. If one can realize this awakening, all things are seen as empty."
Medicine is applied to illness; awakening is applied to delusion; goodness is applied to evil; stillness is applied to movement; wisdom is applied to folly.
All manner of spiritual practices are merely methods of counteractive treatment. Refrain from all evils and strive diligently to do good.
If you practice according to this, you will attain mastery in every direction; how could it be difficult?
Master Fu’s verse says: When Śūnyatā-janman heard the wondrous principle, It was like a thistle growing amidst hemp.

If ordinary people were to believe this Dharma, They would be like lotus flowers in a burning world. Fearing that people might give rise to the view of nihilism, The Great Sage preemptively established what is permitted and what is prohibited.
If one can remain free from all marks, One will certainly enter the House of the Dharma King.
Chan Master Chuanshan said: "If one does not grasp the latter words, the former discourse is difficult to complete.
He then offered this verse: "Difficult, difficult, difficult—like a clear blue sky over level ground. Easy, easy, easy—like falling asleep while still wearing one's clothes.
The steering of a boat rests entirely with the helmsman; Who says that waves and billows arise from the earth?"
If, in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there are sentient beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it,
such persons will be the most rare and extraordinary of all.
Li Wenhui said: "If a person's mind is constantly empty, tranquil, and profoundly pure, remaining unattached to all phenomena;
if they awaken to the mind that dwells nowhere and realize the dharma of non-attainment—this is the foremost rarity."
Chan Master Chuanshu said: "In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; in wearing clothes and eating food—what further matter is there?
He spoke in verse: Ice is not hot; fire is not cold; earth is not wet; water is not dry.
With adamantine feet treading the ground, the flagpole points toward heaven. If one can believe this, look south at the Big Dipper. (Nothing is impossible.)
Why is this? This person has no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span.
Why is that? The mark of self is precisely no-mark; the marks of person, sentient being, and life-span are likewise no-marks.
Why is this? To be free from all marks is what is called the Buddhas.
Li Wenhui said: "That which is 'not a mark' refers to what was previously called 'marklessness,' which clarifies the meaning of emptiness by negating form.
Furthermore, saying it is 'not a mark' means realizing that the four marks—the self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span—have never arisen from the beginning;
therefore, it is called the 'true mark. As for 'leaving all marks and being named a Buddha,' this refers to awakening."
The true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) has no equal; one should know that such a person does not cling to the two extremes, nor does he abide in the middle way.

Being entirely without dwelling, he is called a Buddha. Furthermore, it is said that by being free from marks, one attains pure realization and understands the three emptinesses (trīṇi śūnyatāni), thereby harmonizing with the true mark and reaching ultimate nirvāṇa.
Regarding the meaning of the three emptinesses: the first is the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), and the second is the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
Afterward, it is simply emptiness within emptiness. The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have all realized this principle;

therefore, they are called Buddhas. Chan Master Chuan said: "The heart does not betray others, and the face shows no color of shame. He then offered this verse: "Old bamboo gives birth to new shoots."
New shoots grow from old branches; rain hastens the arrival of travelers. Wind carries a single sail home;
the density of bamboo does not hinder the passing stream, nor do the heights of mountains obstruct the flight of white clouds.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is.

Li Wenhui said: "Regarding 'so it is, so it is,' the Buddha [affirms this] because Subhūti’s understanding of the meaning of emptiness perfectly accords with the Tathāgata’s intent regarding the Dharma."
Chen Xiong said: "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states: 'To be free from all signs of conjunction is called supreme enlightenment.
By the word 'enlightenment' (jue), the Buddha indicates that external enlightenment is free from all signs of existence, while internal enlightenment is free from all signs of emptiness.
To be free from signs within signs, and free from emptiness within emptiness, one attains the wondrous state of true emptiness and signlessness; for this reason, it is so named."
To become a Buddha.
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who hears this sutra and is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear it, you should know that such a person is most rare.
Master Zhao said: "To attain the understanding of the Mahāyāna through the wisdom of hearing is to have no sign of fear in one's person upon first hearing the sutras;

therefore, it is called 'not being startled. To attain the understanding of the Mahāyāna through the wisdom of reflection is to have deep faith and no doubt; therefore, it is called 'not being terrified.
To attain the understanding of the Mahāyāna through the wisdom of cultivation is to practice in accordance with the teachings and never engage in slander; therefore, it is called 'not being afraid.'"
Chen Xiong said: "If one is not startled, there is no mind of doubt; if one is not terrified, there is no mind of fear; if one is not intimidated, there is no mind of retreat.
Li Wenhui said: "To be without startle, terror, or intimidation means the mind is as empty and still as space, profoundly serene and pure."
It is equal to empty space; what cause for alarm or fear could there be?

It is truly rare that those of superior faculties, upon hearing this sutra, listen attentively, receive it, and uphold it without ever regressing. You should know that such persons are exceedingly rare.
Master Fu’s verse says: “If one is able to resolve the mind [for enlightenment], One should understand the two extremes.

Nirvāṇa has no marks; Bodhi is free from objects of perception. [Subcommentary by Zi Rong: When first resolving the mind to practice and cultivating the bodhisattva path, one must seek out those who possess the correct knowledge and vision of the Mahāyāna and have attained realization of the Supreme Vehicle.

Only after first understanding the attachments to the two extremes of existence and non-existence can one realize the principle of the markless nature of nirvāṇa; thus, one becomes detached from the mind and its objects of perception. There is neither vehicle nor rider; [this refers to] person and phenomena.”
Abandon both. To reach the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*), one should recognize the original source.
Chan Master Chuan said: "It is simply that which belongs to oneself. The verse says: A single hair swallows the vast ocean;
A mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru. The full moon hangs over the azure sky; The light of Dharma illuminates the six directions. When you have trodden the fields of your native land with stability,
There is no longer north, south, east, or west.
Why is this? Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is not, in fact, a foremost pāramitā;
it is merely designated as the foremost pāramitā.
The Commentary states: "Why is this so? This reveals that among the causes, [this] is the most supreme.

It clarifies that there are ten types of what are designated as the foremost *pāramitā*: first, generosity; second, ethical discipline; third, patience; fourth, diligence; fifth, meditative concentration.
Sixth is wisdom; seventh is loving-kindness; eighth is compassion; ninth is skillful means; tenth is non-retrogression.
Now, when it is said that the first *pāramitā* is the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving), why is giving alone designated as the foremost?
It is said that giving universally encompasses all practices until one reaches Bodhi; even the practice of the gift of Dharma is based on the support provided by material giving.
Regarding "all virtues," the term "not" is used because one fears the presence of a mind of subject and object;
thus, one first sweeps away provisional names and practices giving without abiding in marks. Therefore, it is said: "This is called the foremost *pāramitā*."
Li Wenhui said: "When the Tathāgata speaks of the 'first pāramitā,' if one awakens to the fact that there are no marks, one immediately reaches the other shore.
Because the true mark is non-dual, it is called the first. As for what is not the first pāramitā:
when one fully realizes that both person and phenomena are empty, there is no birth-and-death to be crossed, nor is there any other shore to be reached. Where else could there be [a shore]?"

Because there is a "first," it is said that this is not the first. That which is called the "first *pāramitā*" refers to awakening to all phenomena (*dharmas*), whereby one realizes that all phenomena are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*). As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "It is only by means of provisional names..."
To guide sentient beings so that they may awaken to this and enter the gate of seeing one's nature is called the first *pāramitā*.
Therefore, know that these are provisional names, like using yellow leaves as gold to stop a small child’s crying.
When those of the Two Vehicles hear it said that these are provisional names, they take them to be real; they cling to them in their practice, desiring to leave birth and death behind.
If one does not know [this], there is no birth and death to be abandoned.

Master Fu’s verse says: "Pāramitā is called 'the other shore'; within it, there are ten names. (In the sixty-sixth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when the youth Sudhana sees the elder Ratnacūḍa, he says:
"I pray that you will explain for me the path of all bodhisattvas. He replies: "The dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, and dhyāna-pāramitā.")

The Prajñāpāramitā, the Upāya-pāramitā, the Praṇidhāna-pāramitā, the Bala-pāramitā, and the Jñāna-pāramitā. Furthermore, the *Jiǔshíliù juǎn hélùn* (Combined Treatise in Ninety-six Volumes) states: "These one hundred and eighteen great dhāraṇī-gates do not transcend the practice of the ten pāramitās.
High and low arise from the conditions of deluded consciousness; they follow one another as objects of ignorance.

It is like seeking water within a mirage, or searching for an echo in the void. How can there be gain or loss regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*)? Only now is it designated as the "Perfectly Accomplished Nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). [Zi Róng said: Regarding True Suchness...]

In principle, from the Buddhas above down to all living beings below, [this nature] is inherently complete. Though one may transmigrate through the six realms, it has never been attained before; that it is now called "perfectly accomplished" (pariniṣpanna) means that upon hearing these words, one realizes immediately that one is a Buddha.
Chan Master Chuansong said in verse: "This is called the foremost *pāramitā*. From it emerge ten thousand distinctions and a thousand variations.
When ghostly faces and divine heads come before one's very eyes, at that moment, do not say you do not recognize them."
Subhūti, the perfection of patience—what the Tathāgata calls the perfection of patience is not a perfection of patience;
it is designated as the perfection of patience.
The *Shuchao* states: "The perfection of patience is the third among the ten perfections."
Wang Rihui said: The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying that it is by being able to endure insults that one does not give rise to anger, which would otherwise cloud and disturb the true nature;
only then can one reach the other shore of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is called the *pāramitā* of patience.
Although the Buddha sometimes refers to himself as the Tathāgata or as the Buddha, there are also times when...
When it says "I," it refers specifically to my own person. When it says "Tathāgata" or "Buddha," it means that this applies equally to myself and all other Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Throughout this entire sutra, it is exactly like this. This Buddha is speaking of the *pāramitā* of patience to me and to all Buddhas;
yet within true nature (*bhūtatathatā*), how could there even be such a thing as patience?
...it is thus. Therefore, it is not real either, but is merely a hollow name. Hence it is said: "This is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Li Wenhui said: As for the perfection of patience, if there is a mind that is able to endure, this is precisely seeing [the truth].
There is the appearance of a body, yet one does not realize that it is devoid of the characteristics of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Master Dayang held up a torch and asked a monk, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "When it arises, it pervades the entire dharma-realm."
When extinguished, there is nothing at all to be attained. Furthermore, Layman Pang asked Mazu, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion?
Mazu replied, "Turn the light back upon yourself and look; wait until you can swallow up the waters of the West River in a single gulp, and then I will tell you.
Master Yuanwu said, "Those who can penetrate this saying..."

At present, all phenomena are stilled and submerged; beginningless deluded thoughts have been utterly cleansed away. It is further said: "The great void has no exterior; the great elephant has no form.
Even if the entire world were brought forth, it would be like a grain of millet; the whole of empty space would be like a pearl in the palm of one's hand."
This can cause the kingdoms of Silla and Persia to clash forehead-to-forehead; it reaches as far as the shooting of arrows from Pūrvavideha to the target in Aparagoyānī.

Thus it is said: "The skull encompasses a thousand worlds; the nostrils touch the monastic wind. Yet, if one has not yet emerged from the realm of the aggregates, one still wanders within seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. To speak in such a manner— *Note: The term "鬬額" (dòu é) refers to a head-to-head confrontation or a decisive struggle. "東勝神洲" (Dōngshèng shénzhōu) is Pūrvavideha, one of the four continents in Buddhist cosmology.

"西瞿耶尼" (Xījūyēní) is Aparagoyānī, another of the four continents. "髑髏" (dúlóu) is the skull. "鼻孔" (bí kǒng) refers to the nostrils. "出家風" (chūjiā fēng) refers to the "monastic wind," implying the authentic spirit or standard of the renunciant life.*
It is just like a duck listening to the sound of thunder, or scratching an itch through a boot.

Even if you were to strip away the sense-bases and their objects, and eliminate all conceptual states and sensory realms, there would still remain a "single thread" of attachment. Furthermore, how can one speak a single phrase that does not involve either of these two paths?
Do you understand? Before the steps of the Buddha Hall is a stone lion; within the vast ocean is an iron Kunlun. Thus spoke the Tathāgata.
Regarding the statement that it is "not the perfection of patience": one who realizes the emptiness of both persons and phenomena (pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā) is without the marks of patience.
This is because they have attained the understanding that the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span do not exist; therefore, it is called "non-patience."

Why is this? Subhūti, when in the past King Kali cut and mangled my body, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span. Why is this?

If, at the time in the past when my limbs were severed joint by joint, I had possessed a perception of a self, a perception of a person, a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a life-span, [then I would have felt aversion].
He gave rise to anger. Subhūti, furthermore, I recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi practicing patience.
During all those lifetimes, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
Master Zhaolun said: "King Kali was an event within the causal conditions of the Tathāgata. At that time, the Bodhisattva had attained the realization of non-self;
this is why he was able to endure [the suffering]. He further said: "The body of the five aggregates does not exist; the four great elements are originally empty.
To bring one's head to the white blade is just like cutting the spring breeze. If one were to consider this through the perspective of the various great masters...
To explain this: it first sets forth the provisional teachings of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and subsequently reveals the ultimate reality of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To express this in terms of symbolic dharma (*dharmaparyāya*): "Song" (*gīta*) is another name for wisdom (*prajñā*). "Sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*) refers to a blade;

This is due to the obscuring darkness of ignorance and the self-concealment of craving; such a person does not awaken to the wondrous principle of true emptiness. It is like a person dwelling in a dark room—"
In the midst of this, all is dark and obscure, and nothing at all is seen. Suppose, however, that the Bodhisattva’s mind and the dharmas both vanish;
thus, dwelling nowhere, they practice giving without aspiration. This is to open wide the adamantine eye.
However, the *Prajñāpradīpa* perfectly awakens to the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision; having realized its own perfection, it is further able to awaken others.
Li Wenhui said: "It is like a person entering darkness, where nothing can be seen. The minds of sentient beings are fundamentally [like this].
Non-abiding. One whose mind is non-abiding perceives the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and is thus called a bodhisattva. Those of the two vehicles dwell their minds within phenomena;
they do not perceive the true reality of all phenomena and turn their backs on the path to enlightenment—how are they different from ordinary worldlings?
It is like a person turning their back on light and entering a dark room; it is like a person with eyes who, when the sunlight shines upon them, perceives various forms.
Those of the Two Vehicles do not see form yet dwell within form, just as one who does not see a pit or a trap falls into that pit or trap.
A Bodhisattva sees form yet does not dwell within form, just as one who sees a pit or a trap does not fall into it.
All dharmas are merely provisional names. Those of the Two Vehicles lack the eye of wisdom and thus cannot distinguish the true from the false;
the Bodhisattva, however, possesses the eye of wisdom and sees that all various forms are entirely without marks.
The Patriarch Bodhidharma said: "Not seeing form is precisely seeing form. Master Xiaoyao said:
"That which is seen may be right or it may be wrong; this is the deluded eye of the world.
That which is neither right nor wrong is the true eye of the world. That which is known may be acceptable or it may be unacceptable; this is the delusion of the world."
The mind is neither capable nor incapable; this is the true mind that transcends the world.

Subhūti, in future ages, if there be good sons or good daughters who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the Tathāgata, by means of the Buddha’s wisdom, will fully know these people and fully see them, all of whom—
One shall attain the accomplishment of immeasurable and boundless merit.
Chen Xiong said: "The 'coming age' refers to the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, namely the ages of the Semblance Dharma and the Final Dharma.
This sutra is a scripture that records the dharma of true emptiness and formlessness. For this sutra to appear in such an age, one must have planted roots of goodness."
The roots [of faith] are difficult to encounter. Even if one is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite them, it should not be merely a matter of oral or auditory study;
rather, it must also involve the profound excellence of mental cultivation. This is what constitutes true capability.
If one is capable in this way, how could the Tathāgata treat me with indifference? He will surely examine me with his unsurpassed knowledge and vision, and thus [the merit] shall be immeasurable.
Boundless merits are all fully accomplished therein. It does not merely benefit a single body, but shall universally bestow upon all sentient beings;
it does not merely benefit a single moment, but shall pervade throughout thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
This is what is called immeasurable and boundless merit.
Yan Bing said: "The Dharma of realizing one's nature attained by the Tathāgata does not belong to the two realms of existence or non-existence;
therefore it is said that it is neither real nor false. If a Bodhisattva’s mind becomes attached to dharmas when practicing giving, this constitutes attachment to signs.
Since this is called attachment to signs, there is no wisdom; it is like a person entering a dark room who sees nothing."
This person practices giving without attachment to phenomena; they penetrate and understand clearly, and thus cannot be deceived by others.
It is like a person who naturally possesses eyes, which, when further illuminated by the light of the sun, perceives all manner of forms and colors with such clarity that nothing remains hidden.
If, in a future age, there are good men or good women who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra—

directly and suddenly awakening to it is called "receiving" (śīla), and practicing it without even momentary abandonment is called "upholding" (dhāraṇa)— they are immediately the Tathāgata of self-nature.
"By means of" means "to employ. To be able to employ the wisdom of the Buddha—what is called this wisdom—is to have penetrating insight into one's nature;

furthermore, it is not the mere cleverness of non-Buddhists. [The Buddhas] fully know these people and fully see these people, and all shall achieve the merit of seeing into their nature, which is immeasurable and boundless.
Li Wenhui said: "The 'future age' refers to the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, specifically the time of the five hundred years of defilement and evil.
Regarding the phrase 'the Tathāgata using the Buddha’s wisdom':

if a person’s mind is constantly diligent in reading and reciting this sutra, their awakened wisdom-nature will gradually open, and they should realize the true mark (dharmatā) of both persons and phenomena."
The two emptinesses are not deluded or disturbed by any objects—whether good or evil, mundane or sagely—and are thus identical to the nature of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
That such a person fully knows and fully sees is something that all Buddhas of the three periods of time do not fail to know or see;
because they have realized awakening, they are able to accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit.
Chan Master Chuanshan said: "One falls because of the ground; one rises because of the ground. What does the ground say to you? He spoke in verse:
"Of the myriad affairs in the world, none are as they usually are; Yet they do not startle, and they endure for a long time.
When things are as usual, it is like the arrival of the autumn wind: Without intention, it cools others, and people cool themselves."
Chapter Ten: On the Merit of Upholding the Sūtra.
Subhūti, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who uphold this sūtra possess merit that is immeasurable.
If, during the first part of the day, such a son or daughter of good family were to offer as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River...

Suppose one were to practice giving during the first part of the day by offering as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and during the middle part of the day, again offer as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;

and during the latter part of the day, likewise offer as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. In this manner, one might offer one's body for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

Yet, if there were another person who, upon hearing this sutra, developed faith and did not oppose it, their merit would surpass that of the former; how much more so if they were to copy, receive, and uphold it?
"Uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others.
Wang Rixiu said: "The 'first part of the day' refers to the early morning; the 'middle part of the day' refers to midday; and the 'latter part of the day' [refers to the afternoon]."
This refers to evening; such is the terminology of the Western lands (India). The Buddha was born therein and thus followed their local dialect.
Nevertheless, even if one gives rise to a single thought of faith in this sutra, the merit obtained is already vast; how much more so if one does so three times a day.
One might give away as many lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons—immeasurable and innumerable.
Although such a person may receive immeasurable rewards of merit, these are merely worldly blessings.
To receive worldly blessings is the cause for being defiled by afflictions, and it is also the cause for committing evil deeds. However, upon hearing this sutra, one’s faith remains uncontradicted.
Thus, one plants these roots of goodness. Once the roots of goodness have been planted, they are said to increase; the longer they endure, the more flourishing they become.
This constitutes supramundane merit; therefore, it cannot be compared with that [worldly merit], but surpasses it immeasurably and infinitely.
Furthermore, how could a person, in three periods of a single day, possibly obtain bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
"Commanding the giving of one's body is merely a metaphorical illustration; it is intended to express, to the utmost, that [the following] cannot be compared to it.

Chen Xiong said: "The Buddha feared that people of the world would cling to the teaching of the Tathāgata’s endurance of insults and would merely give away their bodies, thereby deriving not even a fraction of benefit for their own nature or the nature of others. Therefore, in the thirteenth..."
To speak of it in detail: arriving at this point, he again repeatedly corrects the errors [of previous commentators].
Master Zhao said: "From dawn until the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m. is called the first part of the day; from the hour of the Dragon until the hour of the Sheep (9 a.m.–3 p.m.

is called the middle part of the day; from the hour of the Sheep until the hour of the Dog (3–7 p.m. is called the latter part of the day. Within these three periods, and even unto immeasurable hundreds of thousands [of repetitions]...
Even if one were to sacrifice their body in almsgiving for ten trillion kalpas, it would still not equal the merit of receiving, upholding, and seeing one’s own nature through this sutra.

To see one’s own nature means to profoundly clarify the true mark (*dharmatā*) and realize the emptiness of both persons and phenomena; such a person is truly one who has attained great enlightenment.
Master Fu’s verse says: “Sentient beings and the life-principle (jīva) Are false, empty names superimposed upon the aggregates (skandhas).

Like the hair of a tortoise, they lack substance; Like the horns of a hare, they have no form. (Hanshan’s poem says: “On his body he wears a robe of empty flowers; On his feet he treads shoes of tortoise-hair. In his hand he grasps a bow of hare-horns, Intending to subdue the demon of ignorance. A tortoise originally has no hair, yet it is called ‘tortoise-hair’;

A hare originally has no horns, yet it is called ‘hare-horns. These are all merely false and empty names. Now, upon the five aggregates of sentient beings and the life-principle—how could such things exist? They too are merely false and empty names, yet they are so called.)

To speak of "sentient beings" is to call them "living entities," which is as unreal as the hair of a tortoise and as formless as the horns of a hare. To sacrifice one's body arises from deluded consciousness; to give up one's life stems from confused emotion.
When discussing merit and wisdom in detail, they do not equal the upholding of this sutra.
Li Wenhui said: "To have faith that does not oppose" means to believe in accordance with principle; hence it is called "not opposing. The *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"Gazing up at the Honored Countenance, the eyes do not for a moment abandon it; the mind is always diligent and uninterrupted."

Regarding "upholding, receiving, reading, and reciting": practicing and understanding in accordance with the teaching is called "receiving" (śīla); courageous and diligent effort is called "upholding" (dhāraṇa); the non-distraction of the mind is called "reading" (pāṭha);
and seeing the nature of reality without contradiction is called "reciting" (svādhyāya). Regarding "explaining it for others": [this refers to elucidating the meaning for others].

This means that having personally realized and entered into the ability to see self-nature, one uses skillful means to explain this sutra for others, enabling them to awaken to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and achieve the unsurpassed path.
This constitutes the gift of Dharma; its merit, being free from any abiding characteristic, is boundless.
It surpasses by a hundred thousand million times the merit of giving one's body in alms for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
Chan Master Shuian said: "The blessings and rewards of humans and devas are indeed not lacking, but as for the Buddha-dharma, one has not even dreamed of it. He spoke this verse:
The resolve to give arises equally at the beginning, middle, and end; its merit is boundless and beyond calculation.
How can this compare to the mind of faith that establishes nothing at all—a single blow shatters the vast void?
Subhūti, to state it briefly: this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
Master Zhaolun said: "The merit inherent in this dharma-gate transcends the realm of the mind; therefore, it cannot [be measured]."
It is because it is contemplated by the mind. Since it transcends the realm of speech, it cannot be discussed with the mouth.
Wang Rixiu said: "That which is called 'inconceivable' (acintya) means it cannot be conceived by the mind and cannot be discussed with words.
As for 'incalculable' (atulya), since it has already been stated that it cannot be discussed, then this so-called 'measuring' (tula)—"
It is not a "name" in the sense of verbal designation; rather, it is a "name" in the sense of weighing. In antiquity, the characters for "name" (稱) and "scale" (秤) were used interchangeably.
This means that it cannot be weighed by a scale. That which is "immeasurable" means that it cannot be measured by any physical vessel or instrument.

Yan Bing said: "If one were to perform the practice of giving away one's own body as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River three times each day—'sand' being used here to signify a vast quantity—and were to accumulate such acts of giving for immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, it would not equal the merit of having faith in this sutra and not opposing it.
'Not opposing' means acting in accordance with it; its merit is still able to surpass that of conditioned existence."
What need is there to mention the merit of those who can further resolve their minds to copy, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and explain and expound it for others?
The Buddha speaks of this in brief: this sutra possesses inconceivable and immeasurable qualities;
indeed, even the praises of all Buddhas cannot equal its merit, which is supremely great and boundless.
Li Wenhui said: "Regarding 'boundless merit,' if a person, through this scripture,
realizes the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena and deeply understands the true mark (*dharmatā*), their merit will be vast and great, identical to the Buddha-mind,
without limit and immeasurable."
"The Tathāgata speaks for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna; he speaks for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.
Wang Rihui said: "Vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to a carriage or vehicle. The "Mahāyāna" refers to the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
Arhats alone understand birth and death but do not deliver sentient beings; therefore, it is called the "Hīnayāna," which is like the smallness of a carriage.
The [śrāvaka] can only carry himself alone. The person of the pratyekabuddha is half for others and half for themselves;
thus they constitute the Middle Vehicle, being like a carriage that is moderately sized.
The bodhisattva is one of the Great Vehicle, meaning they are like a large carriage capable of universally carrying and delivering all sentient beings. This sutra intends to deliver all universally.
It is for the sake of all sentient beings that this is taught to those who have set their minds upon the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna. "To set one's mind" (fa) refers to the act of arousing;
to "set one's mind upon the Mahāyāna" means to arouse this vehicle in order to deliver and liberate sentient beings. As for the "Supreme Vehicle" (Agrayāna):

This refers to the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*). Since the Buddha can further encompass and ferry across the bodhisattvas, it stands above the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) and is thus called the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).
Because there is no vehicle superior to this vehicle, it is the most supreme.
Furthermore, this sutra is taught for those who have set out upon the Buddha Vehicle; that is to say, it concerns the Buddha’s transformation and deliverance of the bodhisattvas as well.
This is the principle of this sutra.
Li Wenhui said: "That which is taught for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna is that their wisdom is vast and expansive, enabling them to perceive their own nature."
Form and emptiness are both discarded; one does not cling to either extreme. Since the two extremes do not exist, there is likewise no middle way to be established.
Being unstained by the myriad objects of experience is precisely the path practiced by Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas. This is taught for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle:
they see no defilement to be loathed, nor do they see any purity to be sought. There is nothing to be discarded, nor anything to be discarded.
Nor does one speak of "non-removal," for there is no dwelling that can be dwelt upon; nor does one speak of "non-dwelling.
The measure of the mind is vast and expansive, as open as the great void, without boundaries or limits; this is precisely the stage of the Buddhas of the Supreme Vehicle.
Chan Master Huangbo said: "When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he wished to preach the True Dharma of the One Vehicle;

however, sentient beings did not believe it and instead gave rise to slander, sinking into the sea of suffering. Had he not preached at all, he would have fallen into stinginess and greed, failing to universally bestow the wondrous Way upon sentient beings.
Therefore, he established skillful means and taught that there are three vehicles. These vehicles have great and small capacities, and their attainments are shallow or deep."
"Profound! All are not fixed dharmas; therefore it is said that there is only the Single Vehicle path, while the other two are not the truth.
Master Chuan said: "It is like cutting a handful of silk: with one cut, all are severed. The verse says:
"With one punch, the barrier of the Transformation City is toppled; with one kick, the fortress of Original Wonder is overturned. Walk with confidence toward north, south, east, or west; cease!"
Seeking the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara: This is taught in the Mahāyāna; it is the supreme teaching. One blow leaves a scar;
one palm-grasp leaves a pool of blood.
If there be anyone who can receive, uphold, read, and recite this, and explain it extensively for others, the Tathāgata knows that person fully and sees them completely.
These people shall all achieve immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit.
Such persons as these are indeed bearing the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Xie Lingyun said: "That [the Dharma] does not fall into ruin for a thousand years depends on people to propagate it. To maintain, practice, and bear this burden is the meaning of 'responsibility' (yi).
Li Wenhui said: "To explain it extensively for others so that all people may attain realization through their knowledge and vision is what is meant by 'inconceivable'."
Regarding those who deliberate upon its merit: these are persons of superior capacity who deeply understand this sutra and fully awaken to the Buddha’s intent.

They uphold this Mahayana scripture and explain it for others, causing all students to each perceive the principle of the signless nature of their own essence and to realize that their original source, their own mind, is the Buddha. One should know that the merit of such a person is boundless.
It is beyond measure. Mazu said, "All of you must believe that your own mind is the Buddha;
this mind is itself the Buddha-mind. He further said, "Outside the mind there is no separate Buddha; outside the Buddha there is no separate mind.
Chan Master Baiguo of Foji Temple said, "Mind and mind are the Buddha; the Buddha’s mind and mind are the Buddha-mind. The Buddha and the Buddha are mind and mind; mind and mind are the Buddha-mind."
When the Buddha of the mind is realized, there is not a single thing; it is like the general who quenched his thirst by imagining plum trees.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "If one does not believe that one's own mind is the Buddha, such a thing is impossible. Master Yuanwu said: "The very mind is the Buddha."
This has already been laid bare in eight characters: "Neither Buddha, nor mind. To ask again is to have it pointed out directly before one's face;
do not seek its words, but pass straight through, and only then will you see the ancients' sincere heart, piece by piece.
If you hesitate, you will miss it right before your eyes. Furthermore, the Verse on Mind and Buddha says: "Buddha is mind, and mind is Buddha. Mind and Buddha..."
All that has ever existed is but a delusive thing. If one knows there is neither Buddha nor mind, only then is one the Buddha of the *tathatā*-dharma-body.
Buddha, Buddha, Buddha—there is no form or likeness. A single orb of light contains the myriad phenomena.
The essence-less essence is the true essence; the signless sign is the real sign. It is neither form nor emptiness, yet not non-empty; it is neither moving nor still.
Neither coming nor going; neither different nor the same; neither being nor non-being. Difficult to grasp, difficult to relinquish, and difficult to anticipate.
Internally and externally luminous and clear, it penetrates everywhere. A single Buddha-land exists within a single grain of sand; a single grain of sand contains the great trichiliocosm.
One body and mind are the same as ten thousand; one who knows this must realize the Dharma of no-mind. Neither stained nor pure, this constitutes pure karma.
Amidst the thousandfold aspects of good and evil, there is neither existence nor non-existence—this is precisely Namo Mahākāśyapa.
Chan Master Huangbo said: "You need only eliminate ordinary sentiments and holy states; apart from the mind, there is no other Buddha.
When the Patriarch came from the West, he pointed directly that all people are, in their entirety, Buddhas. Yet you do not recognize this now;
you cling to the ordinary and the holy, gallop outward, and instead become deluded regarding your own mind. This is why I tell you: the mind itself is the Buddha."
If a single thought of worldly emotion arises, one immediately falls into other realms of existence. From beginningless time until this very day, there has been no difference;
there is no distinct dharma, and for this reason it is called the realization of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. Thus, one becomes a bearer of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having heard the sutra and understood its meaning, one practices according to the teaching and extensively explains the signless (*animitta*) to others.

The Dharma enables all practitioners to awaken to and clarify the mind-ground, allowing them to practice the conduct that is signless and unattached, to develop the luminous wisdom within the mind, and to leave behind all worldly afflictions and deluded thoughts, thereby together accomplishing unsurpassed Bodhi.
One should know that such a person carries upon their shoulders the *svabhāva-tathāgata* and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It resides therein.
Within the body. Master Futi’s verse says:

"The imagined nature was understood first; the perfected nature is realized at this time. Relying on unimpeded wisdom from past vehicles, he employs skillful means to exhort others to uphold [the teachings]."
Chan Master Chuanshan said: "To split apart Mount Taihua, one must be the Spirit of Juling. His verse says:

"Heaps of mountains and piles of peaks arrive, Each and every one is but dust and ash. The pupils in his eyes are azure, The breath within his chest is like thunder. When he goes forth, the deserts and passes are stilled;
When he enters the realm, he penetrates with brilliant talent. A single inch-square heart is as vast as the sea— How many times have its waves been seen to clear?"
They go and return. Why is this?
Subhūti, those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span;
they will therefore be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra to others.
Wang Rihui said: "Lè" (樂) is pronounced with the departing tone; it means "to like. "Small teachings" refers to the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The teachings of the non-Buddhists are precisely for the purpose of attachment to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Because they provide various such explanations, they do not accord with this sutra. Therefore, one cannot listen to, receive, read, recite, or explain them for others.
It is said thus.
Chen Xiong remarked: "Small Dharma" refers to the teachings of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna). The *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"Those of dull faculties delight in the Small Dharma," meaning that their aspirations are inferior and they do not give rise to the mind of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). Such persons fall into false views.

They do not know that what is called the Mahāyāna, the supreme vehicle of the Dharma, is entirely contained within this sutra. Not only do they refuse to listen to or recite it, how much less could they explain it for others?
They are attached to the views of self and personhood and have fallen into false views. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Those who seek the Mahāyāna do not fall into false views. This is precisely what is meant.
Li Wenhui said: "Those who delight in minor dharmas possess the capacity of ordinary, dull-witted people; they are unable to listen with faith and extensively study unsurpassed Bodhi.
They merely cultivate merit and wisdom—the laws of cause and effect regarding the cycle of the six realms.
Even if they were to study forcefully, they would cling to their extensive learning and explain it to others; yet when scrutinized by those with clear vision, they will be at a loss for what to do."
A chaotic mess; a total failure. Master Baoning Yong said: "The color and form are exactly like the real thing;
when handled before others, it shines with an extraordinary luster. But when subjected to the fire of further smelting and testing, in the end it is revealed to be nothing but counterfeit silver."
Chan Master Huangbo said: "The minds of people in ancient times were sharp; as soon as they heard a single word, they would immediately cease their learning.

Therefore, they were called 'idle practitioners of the Way who have ceased learning and attained non-action. People of the present day, however, only desire to possess much knowledge and many interpretations."
To extensively seek out the literal meaning and terminology, calling this "cultivation," is not to realize that excessive knowledge and understanding instead become obstructions;
they all become poisonous medicines. One seeks entirely within the realm of arising and ceasing, yet within True Suchness (*tathatā*), none of these things exist at all.
All previous points of understanding must be completely set aside and made empty; this is precisely the Empty Tathāgata-garbha. As it is said:

As for the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), not even a speck of dust can exist within it; this is precisely the Dharma King who shatters all existence appearing in the world. It is also said:
"At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was not the slightest dharma that I could obtain. These words are intended solely to empty your emotional interpretations and intellectual measures.
Simply dissolve and melt away all internal and external attachments until they are exhausted; when there is no longer any dependence or clinging, this is the state of non-action (*amūla*).

The human realm and the teaching-nets of the Three Vehicles are merely medicines prescribed to suit capacities; they are spoken according to what is appropriate and established according to the occasion, each being different.
One need only understand this and will not be deluded.

First of all, one must not cling to the literal meaning within the framework of mind and objects to form an intellectual interpretation. Why is this so? Because, in truth, there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach. I...
This school of the Gate of the Teaching does not deliberate upon such matters; it simply rests the mind and ceases discursive thought, and that is all.
Furthermore, one need not contemplate what preceded or what followed. It is also said: "One who studies Prajñā does not perceive a single dharma that can be attained.

They sever their intent toward the Three Vehicles, for there is only the One True Reality, which cannot be realized or attained. To claim 'I can realize' or 'I can attain' is entirely an overestimation."
Those arrogant people who cast off their robes and departed during the assembly at the Lotus Sutra were all of this ilk. Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Regarding my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I have truly attained nothing; it is merely a matter of silent resonance."
Students should reflect upon this. Simply cease and rely upon the True Dharma (*saddharma*) for practice.

Let go of the four marks—the self, others, sentient beings, and a life-span—and you will not be deluded or disturbed by any external circumstances during your practice. The *Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma* states:

"If you wish to practice, you must rely on the True Dharma. The essence of the mind is free from thought; its characteristics are like empty space, falling neither into the state of a sage nor that of an ordinary person."
Body and mind are equal. One who practices in this way is said to be practicing the True Dharma.
Master Chuan said: "The benevolent see it and call it benevolence; the wise see it and call it wisdom. The verse says:
Not studying as a hero, nor reading books, one wanders laboriously along the long road. The treasure-trove born of one's mother—*Niang-sheng bao-cang*.
I have no use for it; I would rather willingly become an ignorant man who starves to death.
Why should I begrudge others? Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be, it should be honored by all the world—by devas, humans, and asuras.
You should know that such a place is itself a stupa; everyone should pay homage, prostrate, and circumambulate it with reverence.
One scatters various flowers and incense upon that spot.
Chen Xiong said: "In every place" means that the locations where it exists are not limited to one.
If this true scripture exists, it is like a mani-jewel whose auspicious radiance shines brilliantly; thus, for all those in the celestial realm, the human realm, or the *asura* realm...
As for the realm of the asuras, it is a place worthy of offerings; indeed, this very spot is a precious stūpa containing the true-body relics (śarīra) of the Tathāgata.
Who would not pay homage, make offerings, prostrate, and circumambulate it, scattering various flowers and incense upon that site?
These flowers and incenses are those mentioned in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, namely the sumanā flower and the jāti flower.
"Perfumes: these are the fragrance of the *mallikā* flower, the fragrance of the *campaka* flower, and the fragrance of the blue and white lotuses.
