As for those of superior faculties, they attain awakening upon hearing [the teaching] once and master the great *dhāraṇī*; why then would they require such detailed instruction?
Master Xiaoyao said: "On the path of humans and devas, the cultivation of merit comes first; in the sea of birth and death, the cultivation of the Way is urgent.

This is like a bird wishing to fly without wings, or a tree wishing to flourish without roots; how could such things be achieved? It is further said:
"A man of heroic caliber who plots for kingship but fails will still become a hegemon; a hunter who pursues the stag but fails will still catch a hare.

Hehe! I thought there was no one great. The verse says: When hungry, one finds food; when thirsty, one finds drink; when ill, one finds recovery.
The fevered find coolness; the poor encounter treasure; the infant sees its mother; the drifting boat reaches the shore; the solitary traveler returns home. Meeting sweet rain in a drought;

the land possesses loyal and virtuous men. The four barbarian tribes fold their hands in submission; the eight quarters of the world come to surrender. Every single thing is thus; every object is fully revealed.
From the ancients to the present, from ordinary beings to sages, from hell to heaven, and throughout the east, west, south, and north—there is no need for further seeking.

Among the various scriptures of the Great Canon, all that was proclaimed from the Buddha’s own mouth is profoundly deep and subtle.

Yet, this single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā* alone clarifies the nature of delusion, tracing it back to its ultimate source; it serves as a swift path for sentient beings to untangle their attachments and release their fetters.

Consequently, those who receive and uphold it are numerous, and its spiritual efficacy is most manifest. Nevertheless, what circulates in the world consists mostly of the main text alone, while the [commentaries]...

The commentaries on the *Jia* (Family) [section] have not yet been fully perfected. What has been compiled here is particularly essential. Thirty years ago, it was carved at Dongcheng and printed and distributed by Gu Zhai of Ze’an;
however, it soon became stagnant and remained on the shelves. Now, fortunately, the blocks remain intact and have come into the possession of Mr. Wang Jinsi of Jinxi. Mr.
Wang has resolved to print and distribute them, hoping that like-minded colleagues will cooperate to ensure their wide circulation, so that all may read them.
If the reciter merely unrolls this scroll and reaches its profound depths, awakening to its subtle purport—
comprehending the ten thousand practices within the Six Perfections and realizing Bodhi by emptying the four marks— then that single fragment of numinous light within their original nature,
which remains indestructible through accumulated kalpas as firm and sharp as gold, will not have failed me.
The Buddha’s compassion for saving the world is boundless, and thus the merit, practice, and vows of those who print and distribute this work shall likewise be inexhaustible.
Recently, the layman Dai Yinwen presented me with one volume; I was filled with joy and offered praise, joining my palms in reverence and prostrating myself before it.

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* consist of six hundred fascicles; the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra* is but one fascicle among them. Yet, the profound and secret truth of the Nature School (*Xingzong*) is fully encompassed therein.
Its great essentials take "generating the mind through non-abiding" as its ultimate resort. For non-abiding is emptiness.
Whatever mind arises does not fall into inert emptiness. By what means does one enter this gate? By means of the six suchnesses (*ṣaḍ-tathatā*), one is free from the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
Thus one achieves patience (*kṣānti*) and abides in suchness (*tathatā*) without movement; having already ascended to the other shore, it is said in two parts:
"One should give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; one should abide thus and thus subdue the mind. This is the place of its arising.
This is precisely the place of descent; it is also the place of abiding. That is to say, "the very moment is it. To turn one's thought away from this is to deviate from it.
